First Aid for Electric Shock
Immediate Response Before Medical Help Arrives
An electric shock happens when the body comes into contact with a live source of electrical current, such as faulty wiring, a damaged appliance, or a power line. The danger depends on the voltage, the current's path through the body, and how quickly help is given. Damage may not always be visible on the skin, since an electric current can injure the heart, muscles, and internal organs even when there is no obvious burn. Every electric shock, however minor it seems, deserves caution and medical evaluation.
What to Do Immediately
1. Do not touch the person if they are still in contact with the electrical source. Touching them directly could pass the current through you as well.
2. Turn off the power at the source if possible, such as the switch, circuit breaker, or fuse box, before approaching the person.
3. If the power cannot be turned off, separate the person from the source using a dry, non-conducting object such as a wooden stick, plastic broom handle, or thick dry rope. Stand on a dry surface such as a wooden board, rubber mat, or stack of dry newspapers while doing this.
4. Once the person is safely away from the electrical source, check whether they are conscious and breathing. Call out to them and gently check for a response.
5. If the person is not breathing or shows no signs of movement, coughing, or response, begin CPR immediately if you are trained, and continue until help arrives or the person recovers.
6. If the person is breathing but unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side) to keep the airway clear, and continue monitoring them.
7. Cover any visible burns loosely with a clean, dry, sterile dressing or cloth. Do not use a fluffy towel or blanket directly on a burn, since loose fibers can stick to the wound.
8. Keep the person warm and as still as possible, and continue watching their breathing, pulse, and responsiveness closely until emergency responders arrive.
What NOT to Do
• Do not touch the person while they are still in contact with the electrical current, even to try to help them; you risk being shocked yourself.
• Do not use any metal, wet material, or damp cloth to move the person or the electrical source away, as these conduct electricity.
• Do not approach downed power lines or high-voltage wires under any circumstances; stay well back and wait for the power company or emergency services to confirm the power is off.
• Do not move the person unnecessarily unless they are in immediate danger, such as fire or ongoing electrical contact.
• Do not pour water, apply ointments, ice, or butter to an electrical burn.
• Do not assume the person is fine just because there is no visible burn or they seem alert; internal damage, including to the heart, may not show right away.
• Do not give the person food or water, in case medical treatment or anesthesia is needed soon after.
• Do not delay calling for emergency help while attempting first aid; if you are alone, call for help as soon as the person is safely away from the current, or as you begin care if a phone is nearby.
When to Call Emergency Services
Call an ambulance (108 in India, or the local emergency number) immediately if any of the following apply:
• The person has lost consciousness, is not breathing normally, or shows no signs of circulation.
• The shock came from a high-voltage source, a power line, or lightning.
• There are visible burns, especially if they appear deep, widespread, or are on the face, hands, feet, or genitals.
• The person has chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, difficulty breathing, or seizures.
• The person appears confused, disoriented, or has persistent muscle pain, numbness, or weakness.
• The shock passed through the chest, or you are unsure how severe the current or exposure was.
• Any electric shock has occurred in a child, elderly person, or pregnant woman, since even a seemingly mild shock warrants prompt medical review.
• You are unsure whether the shock was serious, since even a shock that looks minor can cause hidden internal or cardiac injury that needs medical evaluation.
Source Basis
This guidance reflects general first-aid principles for electric shock as commonly described by established public health and emergency medicine organizations, including recognized international and Indian emergency care bodies. It is a general awareness summary in original wording and is not a substitute for certified first-aid training or professional medical instructions.
